{{Short description|Complexity class}}
In [[computational complexity theory]], the [[complexity class]] '''PPP''' ('''polynomial pigeonhole principle''') is a subclass of [[TFNP]]. It is the class of search problems that can be shown to be total by an application of the [[pigeonhole principle]]. [[Christos Papadimitriou]] introduced it in the same paper that introduced PPAD and PPA.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Christos Papadimitriou | year = 1994 | title = On the complexity of the parity argument and other inefficient proofs of existence | journal = [[Journal of Computer and System Sciences]] | volume = 48 | issue = 3 | pages = 498–532 | url = http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~christos/papers/On%20the%20Complexity.pdf | doi = 10.1016/S0022-0000(05)80063-7 | access-date = 2009-12-11 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084618/http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~christos/papers/On%20the%20Complexity.pdf | archive-date = 2016-03-04 | url-status = dead }}</ref> PPP contains both [[PPAD]] and PWPP (polynomial weak pigeonhole principle) as subclasses. These complexity classes are of particular interest in cryptography because they are strongly related to cryptographic primitives such as [[One-way function|one-way permutations]] and [[Collision resistance|collision-resistant hash functions]].

==Definition==

PPP is the set of all function computation problems that admit a [[polynomial-time reduction]] to the ''PIGEON'' problem, defined as follows:

:Given a [[Boolean circuit]] <math>C</math> having the same number <math>n</math> of input bits as output bits, find either an input <math>x</math> that is mapped to the output <math>C(x) = 0^n</math>, or two distinct inputs <math>x \ne y</math> that are mapped to the same output <math>C(x) = C(y)</math>.

A problem is PPP-[[Complete (complexity)|complete]] if ''PIGEON'' is also polynomial-time reducible to it. Note that the pigeonhole principle guarantees that ''PIGEON'' is total. We can also define ''WEAK-PIGEON'', for which the
weak pigeonhole principle guarantees totality. PWPP is the corresponding class of problems that are polynomial-time reducible to it.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Emil Jeřábek | year = 2016 | title = Integer factoring and modular square roots | journal = [[Journal of Computer and System Sciences]] | volume = 82 | issue = 2 | pages = 380–394 | doi = 10.1016/j.jcss.2015.08.001| arxiv = 1207.5220 }}</ref> ''WEAK-PIGEON'' is the following problem:

:Given a Boolean circuit <math>C</math> having <math>n</math> input bits and <math>n-1</math> output bits, find <math>x \ne y</math> such that <math>C(x) = C(y)</math>.

Here, the range of the circuit is strictly smaller than its domain, so the circuit is guaranteed to be non-[[Injective function|injective]]. ''WEAK-PIGEON'' reduces to ''PIGEON'' by appending a single 1 bit to the circuit's output, so PWPP <math>\subseteq</math> PPP.

== Generalized pigeonhole principles ==

The ordinary PIGEON problem can be viewed equivalently as finding a collision in a map from <math>N+1</math> pigeons to <math>N</math> holes. This has been generalized to multi-collisions. For an integer <math>t \ge 2</math>, the problem <math>t</math>-PIGEON asks, given a Boolean circuit representing a map from <math>(t-1)N+1</math> pigeons to <math>N</math> holes, to find <math>t</math> distinct pigeons mapped to the same hole. The associated class <math>t</math>-PPP consists of total NP search problems reducible to this problem; <math>2</math>-PPP coincides with PPP.<ref name="JainLiRobereXun2024">{{cite conference |last1=Jain |first1=Siddhartha |last2=Li |first2=Jiawei |last3=Robere |first3=Robert |last4=Xun |first4=Zhiyang |title=On Pigeonhole Principles and Ramsey in TFNP |book-title=2024 IEEE 65th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) |year=2024 |publisher=IEEE |pages=406–428 |doi=10.1109/FOCS61266.2024.00033 |arxiv=2401.12604}}</ref>

Jain, Li, Robere, and Xun studied these classes as a hierarchy of generalized pigeonhole principles.<ref name="JainLiRobereXun2024" /> They proved that, in the black-box setting, the generalized pigeonhole classes form a strict hierarchy and related them to multi-collision resistance in cryptography. They also showed that as a consequence, RAMSEY (given a graph, find a clique or independent set of a size guaranteed to exist) does not have a black-box reduction to PPP. This was evidence towards refuting a conjecture by Goldberg and Papadimitriou that RAMSEY is in the class PPP in the standard circuit model. 

==Connection to cryptography==

We can view the circuit in ''PIGEON'' as a polynomial-time computable hash function. Hence, PPP is the complexity class which captures the hardness of either inverting or finding a collision in hash functions. More generally, the relationship of subclasses of [[FNP (complexity)|FNP]] to polynomial-time complexity classes can be used to determine the existence of certain cryptographic primitives, and vice versa.

For example, it is known that if FNP = [[Function problem|FP]], then [[one-way functions]] do not exist. Similarly, if PPP = FP,
then one-way permutations do not exist.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Christos Papadimitriou | year = 1994 | title = On the complexity of the parity argument and other inefficient proofs of existence | journal = [[Journal of Computer and System Sciences]] | volume = 48 | issue = 3 | pages = 498–532 | url = http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~christos/papers/On%20the%20Complexity.pdf | doi = 10.1016/S0022-0000(05)80063-7 | access-date = 2009-12-11 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084618/http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~christos/papers/On%20the%20Complexity.pdf | archive-date = 2016-03-04 | url-status = dead }}</ref> Hence, PPP (which is a subclass of FNP) more closely captures the question of the existence of one-way permutations. We can prove this by reducing the problem of inverting a permutation <math>\pi</math> on an output <math>y</math> to ''PIGEON''. Construct a circuit <math>C</math> that computes <math>C(x) = \pi(x) \oplus y</math>. Since <math>\pi</math> is a permutation, a solution to ''PIGEON'' must output <math>x</math> such that <math>C(x) = 0 = \pi(x) \oplus y</math>, which implies <math>\pi(x) = y</math>.

Multi-collision resistance gives a cryptographic analogue of generalized pigeonhole principles. For <math>t \ge 2</math>, a <math>t</math>-multi-collision-resistant hash function (<math>t</math>-MCRH) is a shrinking keyed hash family for which it is computationally infeasible to find <math>t</math> distinct inputs with the same output; <math>2</math>-MCRH is ordinary collision resistance. The associated search problem is a weak <math>t</math>-collision pigeonhole problem, often denoted <math>t</math>-PWPP, and is closely related to the non-weak hierarchy <math>t</math>-PPP.<ref name="JainLiRobereXun2024">{{cite conference |last1=Jain |first1=Siddhartha |last2=Li |first2=Jiawei |last3=Robere |first3=Robert |last4=Xun |first4=Zhiyang |title=On Pigeonhole Principles and Ramsey in TFNP |book-title=2024 IEEE 65th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) |year=2024 |publisher=IEEE |pages=406–428 |doi=10.1109/FOCS61266.2024.00033 |arxiv=2401.12604}}</ref>

Jain, Li, Robere, and Xun described their black-box separations among generalized pigeonhole principles as a first step toward the cryptographic question of whether multi-collision resistance can be generically converted into ordinary collision resistance.<ref name="JainLiRobereXun2024" /> Subsequent work of Mao and Zhang resolved the fully black-box adjacent-step version of this question: for every constant <math>t \ge 3</math>, there is no black-box construction of <math>(t-1)</math>-MCRH from <math>t</math>-MCRH.<ref name="MaoZhang2026">{{cite report |last1=Mao |first1=Xinyu |last2=Zhang |first2=Jiapeng |title=Black-Box Separation Between Multi-Collision Resistance and Collision Resistance |institution=Electronic Colloquium on Computational Complexity |number=TR26-046 |date=5 April 2026 |url=https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2026/046/}}</ref> Under the usual translation between fully black-box cryptographic constructions and randomized black-box Turing reductions between the associated search problems, this rules out the corresponding reduction from the <math>t</math>-collision pigeonhole problem to the <math>(t-1)</math>-collision problem; in particular, it rules out a fully black-box construction of ordinary collision-resistant hashing from 3-multi-collision-resistant hashing.<ref name="MaoZhang2026" />

==Relationship to PPAD==

PPP contains [[PPAD]] as a subclass (strict containment is an [[open problem]]). This is because ''End-of-the-Line'', which defines PPAD, admits a straightforward polynomial-time reduction to ''PIGEON''. In ''End-of-the-Line'', the input is a start vertex <math>s</math> in a [[directed graph]] <math>G</math> where each vertex has at most one successor and at most one predecessor, represented by a polynomial-time computable [[successor function]] <math>f</math>. Define a circuit <math>C</math> whose input is a vertex <math>x</math> and whose output is its successor if there is one, or <math>x</math> if it does not. If we represent the source vertex <math>s</math> as the bitstring <math>0^n</math>, this circuit is a direct reduction of ''End-of-the-Line'' to ''Pigeon'', since any collision in <math>C</math> provides a sink in <math>G</math>.

==Notable problems==

===Equal sums problem===

The equal sums problem is the following problem. Given <math>n</math> positive integers that sum to less than <math>2^n - 1</math>, find two distinct subsets of the integers that have the same total. This problem is contained in PPP, but it is not known if it is PPP-complete.

===Constrained-SIS problem===

The constrained-SIS (short integer solution) problem, which is a generalization of the [[Short integer solution problem|SIS problem]] from [[lattice-based cryptography]], has been shown to be complete for PPP.<ref>{{cite conference | author = K. Sotiraki, M. Zampitakis, and G. Zirdelis | title = PPP-Completeness with Connections to Cryptography | book-title = Proc. of 59th [[Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science]] | year = 2018 | pages = 148–158 | doi = 10.1109/FOCS.2018.00023 | arxiv = 1808.06407 }}</ref> Prior to that work, the only problems known to be complete for PPP were variants of ''PIGEON''.

===Integer factorization===

There exist polynomial-time randomized reductions from the [[integer factorization]] problem to ''WEAK-PIGEON''.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Emil Jeřábek | year = 2016 | title = Integer factoring and modular square roots | journal = [[Journal of Computer and System Sciences]] | volume = 82 | issue = 2 | pages = 380–394 | doi = 10.1016/j.jcss.2015.08.001| arxiv = 1207.5220 }}</ref> Additionally, under the [[generalized Riemann hypothesis]], there also exist deterministic polynomial reductions. 
However, it is still an open problem to unconditionally show that integer factorization is in PPP.
